title: Seventy times seven (Matthew 18:21–35)
hook: the same apology, on repeat. Peter wants a number
tomorrow: why would Jesus' own friends shoo the children away?

segments.voice: Yesterday, where two or three: go alone first, to gain your brother back, and the promise of the small room: there am I. Peter was listening. He has a follow-up.

Some hurts come back on repeat: the same late text, the same forgotten promise, the same eye-roll. Peter wants to know how long he has to keep forgiving. So he asks for a number, and offers a generous one: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" Jesus answers: "I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." Then he tells a story about why the counting won't work.
screen: `THE SAME HURT, ON REPEAT.` → `TILL SEVEN TIMES?` → `UNTIL SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN.`

segments.voice: A king settles accounts. One servant owes ten thousand talents, a debt no one could ever pay. He falls down and begs: "Lord, have patience with me, and I will pay thee all." And the king does more than wait. He "was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt." All of it. That same servant walks out, finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred pence, and grabs him by the throat: "Pay me that thou owest." The man begs him in almost the same words: have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. He won't hear it, and throws him in prison. The king calls him back: "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" Here's what this week might need from it. The servant had been forgiven everything and still couldn't forgive a little, because he never let the first mercy change him. And notice what Jesus does not say. The same chapter began with naming the fault out loud. Forgiving again isn't pretending it never happened. Seventy times seven isn't a bigger number to track. It's the end of tracking.
screen: `TEN THOUSAND TALENTS, FORGIVEN.` · `A HUNDRED PENCE, NOT FORGIVEN.` · `SHOULDEST NOT THOU ALSO?` · `NOT PRETENDING: NOT COUNTING.` · then, large: `AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper. Write the initial of someone you've had to forgive for the same thing more than once, and under it, two words: and again. Fold it and hold it in your hand for the sit; it's not a promise to feel anything yet, just the start of not counting.
Seventy times seven. Jesus' answer to Peter's count: not a bigger number, the end of the ledger.
The line to take with you: and again, because the king forgave the whole debt first. That’s today.

fork.setup: a coworker covered for you on a huge mistake last month. today a new hire gets your order wrong, and you're about to snap. what would the parable ask first?
options: remember what was forgiven you, and let it change how you answer.
point out the mistake firmly, so it doesn't happen again.
say nothing now, and keep a note in case it happens twice.
fork.reveal: the servant forgiven ten thousand talents wouldn't forgive a hundred pence. the king's question: shouldest not thou also have had compassion?

original.note: Greek: to forgive, to let go; the verb in Peter's question in Matthew 18:21.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgive 490 times, then you're done.
what it means: stop counting; let the mercy you've received change how you treat others.
what a scholar hears: Peter's seven was already generous; seventy times seven answers it, and the talents and pence set an impossible debt beside a small one.
guess: a fixed limit on how often to forgive
a prophecy counting years until the end

chat.says: talked to Kayla alone. she said sorry. today she did the eye-roll during my solo again. forgive again??
options: And again. Jesus ends the counting, not the honesty: forgive, and still name it if it repeats.
Not yet. Seven times is the number Peter suggested, and she's only used two chances.
Yes, and act like it never happened. Forgiving means you never bring it up again.
chat.meaning: Seventy times seven ends the tracking. The same chapter starts by naming the fault to the person alone; forgiving again isn't pretending.

talents.meaning: a huge sum of money in the story, far beyond paying back

pence.meaning: the King James word for small coins, a modest sum

fellowservant.meaning: a servant of the same master

Shouldest.meaning: older English for should you, or shouldn't you

notes: The parable's hard ending (the servant delivered to the tormentors, 18:34–35, forgiveness 'from your hearts') is cited but not retold, for length and tone; a Keeper may want one line restored.

'Forgiving again isn't pretending it never happened' rests on Matthew 18:15 (naming the fault), the same chapter. Confirm the framing; it is offered so the lesson never pressures someone to stay in harm. A parent/abuse caveat may belong in a later lesson.
'Seventy times seven': the Greek can also be read 'seventy-seven times'; not raised, to keep to the KJV text. 490 appears only in the myth item as the popular misreading.
Life shape: the chat leads. Grace storyline, day 5: she talked to Kayla alone (between days); Kayla apologized, then rolled her eyes again. The right reply: forgive again and still be honest.
